Gomez , Lukasz Kaiser , Illia Polosukhin ... Abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks in an encoder-decoder configuration. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to- German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles by over 2 BLEU.

contexts.text: Third, we provide a hybrid agent decision architecture that decouples game-theoretic base behaviour from LLM narrative response, enabling reproducible evalua- tion of LLM-mediated coordination at the system level. Fourth, we provide cross-backbone evidence (Section 4.7) that the framework is model-agnostic across five contemporary LLMs in both homogeneous and heterogeneous configurations, a property of practical importance for systems integrators who cannot assume uniform LLM provisioning across coordinator and agent layers.   The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on LLM-based multi-agent coordination, evolutionary cooperation on networks, and con- stitutional alignment. Section 3 describes the experimental framework, covering the hy- brid agent decision model, personality archetypes, governance pipeline, and ECS metric. Section 4 presents the four experiments and results. Section 5 interprets the autonomy para- dox, the resistance–governance complementarity, and design implications for intelligent generative systems. Section 6 concludes.   2. Related Work LLM-powered agents have moved from proof-of-concept simulations to architectures   with practical coordination functions [1,2]. Park et al. [4] showed that such agents sustain coherent social behaviour over long horizons and develop emergent norms that mirror human communities.

contexts.text: The ability of LLMs to generate contextually rich, persona-aware narratives makes them natural candidates for this coordination role [4–6], and recent work has shown that structured, compiled influence policies outperform unstruc- tured messaging in moving population-level cooperation rates [7]. Yet this same expressive power creates a dual-use risk that is amplified at deployment scale: the mechanisms that enable effective coordination can equally serve manipulation, substituting fear-based fram- ing or misleading factual claims for transparent persuasion, and the electronic system that hosts the coordinator becomes the channel through which manipulation reaches its targets.   The tension is sharpest when the agents are themselves LLM-powered entities rather than passive numerical responders. Empirical studies of LLMs in strategic settings [8–11] report context-conditioned reasoning, episodic memory, and heterogeneous persuasion resistance that depends on personality, history, and perceived credibility. A policy that lands cleanly on an idealised responder may either be flagged and rejected by a grounded agent sensitised by its own reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) alignment, or exploit a cooperative prior in ways that silently degrade system-level fairness and integrity. Whether a system-level filter can hold ethical coordination quality against agents that exercise this kind of independent judgement is therefore the foundational design question for any trustworthy LLM multi-agent stack.

The field has developed several distinct communication architectures including four primary patterns: layered, decentralized, centralized, and shared message pools [119, 436]. contexts.text: Conclusions Constitutional governance of LLM influence policies is a practical and effective mech-   anism for ensuring ethical coordination in generative multi-agent systems. Across ad- versarial and benign environments, governed agents consistently achieve ECS = 0.176 against an unconstrained baseline of ECS = 0, with no cooperation cost under benign conditions and full adversarial threat absorption at pviol = 0.65. The framework is modular, model-agnostic, and deployable as a thin coordination layer over any LLM-powered agent population, making it directly applicable to intelligent workflow automation, decision- support systems, and human–AI collaborative platforms. The headline numerical claims rest on multi-seed bootstrap validation (Section 4.6) and a cross-backbone sweep spanning five contemporary LLM families (Section 4.7), placing the empirical ordering on a broader footing than a single-seed, single-backbone evaluation would provide. question: why should earlier human-AI interaction research findings be reconsidered when studying modern AI systems?
reference: Modern AI systems have significantly different capabilities compared to earlier systems. Therefore, previous research findings may not accurately reflect interactions with today's more advanced AI systems and should be reevaluated.

message.content: Earlier human-AI interaction research findings should be reconsidered when studying modern AI systems because the substrate of interaction has changed so fundamentally that earlier results cannot be assumed to generalize without re-examination. The rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs) and the shift to natively multimodal architectures have altered the conditions under which interaction unfolds in ways that challenge the generalizability of earlier findings. This shift presents a methodological and conceptual inflection point, requiring a recalibration of research for systems that now respond with increasingly social fluidity and complexity.

contexts.text: Third, longitudinal, in-the-wild studies are critical. Documenting usage patterns over months (rather than novelty effects over brief interactions) will be necessary to under stand how engagement stabilizes, or shifts, with long-term use. Fourth, as interactional behavior becomes increasingly human-like, HAI research risks working against null effects when relying on binary comparisons between humans and AI. Studies must introduce multiple, theoretically motivated dimensions of comparison, focusing on specific social and functional mechanisms through which these interactions are organized (see Bai et al., 2025; He et al., 2025). The field should further embrace mixed methods. Rich, qualitative data can reveal the nuances of experience that statistics alone cannot uncover.   On a separate note, the pace of technological deployment raises a complementary challenge. Early research on social media, for example, lagged behind widespread adoption, limiting the field's ability to anticipate long-term effects and impact policy (Orben & Matias, 2025). In this context, practices that support faster scholarly communication, such as the use of preprints, may play an important role in enabling earlier critique, replication, and coordination across the field.   Finally, this shift presents an opportunity. With models that can sustain naturalistic dialogue, HAI research will gain a new window into how humans negotiate agency, trust, and meaning.

contexts.text: Human-AI interaction (HAI) research may now face an analogous challenge to that in AI design. A generation of empirical studies has investigated how people engage with social robots lacking advanced verbal communication (e.g., Kory Westlund & Breazeal, 2015; Tanaka et al., 2007) and voice assistants such as Siri, Alexa, or Google Home (Lovato et al., 2019; Mavrina et al., 2022; Oranç & Ruggeri, 2021).   While impressive for its time, these voice assistants (built on modular pipelines and outdated language models) offered a very different sub strate of interaction than today's systems, and are perhaps better described as interactive tools that you need to get used to than social agents that interacts naturally (Andries & Robertson, 2023; Kim & Choudhury, 2021; Mavrina et al., 2022; Pradhan et al., 2019). The rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs) and the more recent shift to natively multimodal (voice-capable) architectures have altered the conditions under which interaction unfolds in ways that challenge the generalizability of earlier findings. Just as Sutton observed in core AI research, HAI research may also discover that the knowledge accumu lated under the previous technological era has limited applications once the system's capacities make qualitative shifts.

How people engage with contemporary AI fundamentally differs from what previous technologies could offer (Zao-Sanders, 2025). In Kuhn's terms, the field may be experiencing a paradigm shift, understood here as a potential methodological and conceptual inflection point rather than an already consolidated reorganization of HAI. The substrate of interaction has changed so fundamentally that earlier results cannot be assumed to generalize without re-examination. The lesson for HAI is thus method ological humility: to recognize that older findings may not travel across paradigms, and to recalibrate research for systems that now respond with increasingly social fluidity and complexity.   Moving forward, HAI research must adapt accordingly. First, repli cation is essential. Canonical findings must be revisited under these new conditions, and a more careful historical situating of prior work is needed. Second, research design must prioritize longevity. Rather than overfitting to transient model capabilities, studies should model how interaction evolves as systems improve. Third, longitudinal, in-the-wild studies are critical. Documenting usage patterns over months (rather than novelty effects over brief interactions) will be necessary to under stand how engagement stabilizes, or shifts, with long-term use.

question: What is the Bitter Lesson and how has it influenced the development of AI?
reference: he Bitter Lesson shows that general methods relying on increased computational power and data can outperform approaches based on predefined human knowledge. This has influenced the development of modern AI systems.

message.content: The Bitter Lesson, articulated by Richard Sutton in 2019, highlights that research relying on embedding human knowledge into AI systems consistently underperformed compared to general methods that scale with increases in computation. This lesson has significantly influenced the development of AI by shifting the focus from knowledge-driven approaches to domain-general methods that leverage large datasets and computational power. This paradigm shift has enabled the creation of technologies like large language models with native multimodal capabilities, which are reshaping human-AI interaction (HAI). The Bitter Lesson suggests that findings from earlier, technically constrained systems may not generalize to contemporary AI systems, necessitating replication and historical contextualization in HAI research.

contexts.text: A qualitative shift in AI capabilities: A “bitter lesson” for human-AI interaction research?   Kim Astor Uppsala University, Department of Psychology, Sweden   A B S T R A C T   Richard Sutton's “Bitter Lesson” (2019) describes how prior knowledge-driven approaches to AI design were displaced by domain-general methods that scale with data and computation, rendering many prior insights obsolete. The technologies this shift enabled, including large language models with native multimodal ca pabilities, may now reshape human–AI interaction (HAI). Contemporary systems capable of fluid, expressive, open-ended interaction differ not only in degree but in kind from earlier technologies. This paper argues that HAI research may face its own “bitter lesson”: findings derived from interaction with earlier, technically constrained, systems cannot be assumed to generalize without replication and historical contextualization. It situates these developments in relation to methodo logical strategies and the challenges posed by rapid technological change, while highlighting how contemporary AI systems can offer a new lens on human connection and the expression of intelligence.   The most cited lesson in the history of artificial intelligence (AI) is Richard Sutton's “Bitter Lesson” (2019). Sutton argued that across do mains, from chess to vision, research that has relied on embedding human knowledge into systems consistently underperformed compared to general methods that scale with increases in computation.

contexts.text: This paper addresses these gaps by first establishing a clear historical context (Figure 1), which delineates the evolution of AI through five distinct but overlapping eras.   2Figure 1: Historical Evolution of AI Paradigms: This timeline charts the key breakthroughs and eras in AI, from early symbolic systems to the modern agentic era. It highlights the Transformer architecture as the pivotal enabling technology for large language models (LLMs), which in turn powered the generative AI revolution and provided the substrate for contemporary agentic systems.   3The Symbolic AI Era (1950s–1980s) [13] established the foundational ambition of artificial intelligence, grounded in logic and explicit human knowledge. This period was dominated by rule-based systems and expert systems such as MYCIN and DENDRAL [14], which operated on carefully hand-crafted symbolic rules. Intelligence was conceived as a top-down, deductive process, representing the purest form of the symbolic paradigm.   The Machine Learning (ML) Era (1980s–2010s) [15, 16, 17] marked a pivotal shift away from hard-coded logic toward systems that could learn from data. While still heavily dependent on human-engineered features, this period introduced statistical ML models such as Support Vector Machines and decision trees, which powered applications ranging from classification to recommendation.
